solution.concept_anchor: Fresco-secco vs. Tanjore painting — technique and period distinction
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because it correctly names 'Chola murals' and 'fresco technique' in the same sentence, and students who know Chola murals exist at Brihadeeswarar may accept this as the right identification without recognising that the described technique (gold foil, wooden board, rich pigments) is NOT fresco but Tanjore painting.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes: portable works, wooden boards, gold foil overlay, semi-precious stones, vivid natural pigments — these are the hallmarks of Tanjore painting, NOT fresco murals.
Eliminate option (a): Stone carving relief is a three-dimensional sculptural technique — the scenario describes flat portable paintings on wooden boards.
Eliminate option (b): Chola murals are wall paintings (fresco-secco on plaster) — not portable works on wooden boards with gold foil. The scenario's description is incompatible with fresco technique.
Eliminate option (c): Miniature painting on palm leaf uses palm leaf as substrate and is associated with Odishan and Rajasthani traditions — not gold foil on wooden boards.
Confirm option (d): Gold foil, semi-precious stones, vivid pigments on wooden boards = Tanjore painting, developed under Nayaka and Maratha patronage (16th–19th century CE).
solution.final_explanation:
This scenario tests the ability to identify an artistic technique from its material description — a classic application question where surface familiarity with Chola art history is insufficient.

**Applicable principle:** The described technique — portable works on wooden boards, gold foil overlay, embedded semi-precious stones, rich natural pigments — is the defining visual vocabulary of Tanjore (Thanjavur) painting, which developed under Nayaka and Maratha patronage in the 16th–19th centuries CE. It is entirely distinct from the Chola mural tradition.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Stone relief carving is a three-dimensional sculptural process; the scenario describes flat, portable two-dimensional painted works.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Chola murals at Brihadeeswarar are wall-bound, painted on dry plaster (fresco-secco), not on wooden boards, and they do not use gold foil or gem inlays. The portable and gold-embellished nature of the described works rules out the Chola mural tradition.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Palm-leaf miniature paintings use palm leaf as their substrate and are associated with Odisha, eastern India, and some South Indian manuscript traditions — not gold foil on wooden boards.
• Option (d) — Correct: Tanjore painting's signature features are exactly as described: wooden board substrate, glass or semi-precious stone inlay for ornamentation, gold foil for halos and jewellery, and bright natural pigments for the figures. This tradition flourished at Thanjavur under the Nayakas and especially under the Thanjavur Maratha rulers.

Value Addition:
• Tanjore paintings most commonly depict Hindu deities — especially Vishnu/Krishna and Lakshmi — in a frontal, icon-like format.
• The gold-foil technique creates the characteristic glittering surface that distinguishes Tanjore painting from all other Indian painting styles.
• The Nayaka period at Thanjavur (16th–17th century CE) also saw major contributions to Carnatic music and Bharatanatyam codification.

solution.concept_anchor: Rajarajeshvaram — original name of Brihadeeswarar temple
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because 'Peruvudaiyar Kovil' is an actual local name used for Brihadeeswarar in Tamil, and students who have encountered this name may be uncertain whether it or Rajarajeshvaram was the original formal name given by the patron king.
elimination_logic: The question asks for the original name given to the Thanjavur Brihadeeswarar by its patron king as recorded in the temple's own inscriptions.
Eliminate option (c): 'Dakshina Meru Prasadam' is a descriptive epithet ('gift of the southern Meru') that appears as a poetic description — not the formal name given in inscriptions.
Eliminate option (d): 'Shivapadashekara Kshetram' combines the king's personal devotional title with a generic term — this is a fabricated formal name.

Evaluate options (a) and (b): 'Rajarajeshvaram' (temple of the lord of Rajaraja) is the name recorded in the Brihadeeswarar inscriptions as the original formal name. 'Peruvudaiyar Kovil' is a colloquial Tamil name meaning 'temple of the great lord' — authentic, but not the formal inscriptional name. Answer is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (d) 'Shivapadashekara Kshetram' is a plausible-fabrication trap: it combines two authentic elements (Shivapadashekara is Rajaraja Chola I's real title; Kshetram is a real Sanskrit/Tamil word for a sacred site) into a convincing but non-existent formal name. Students who know both components will find this option authoritative-sounding. The actual inscriptional name 'Rajarajeshvaram' (Rajaraja's Ishvara/temple) is the verifiable answer from the primary source.
solution.final_explanation:
The original formal name of the Brihadeeswarar temple, as recorded in its own inscriptions, is an important primary-source detail.

• Option (a) — Correct: The Thanjavur temple was originally called 'Rajarajeshvaram' — 'the temple of Rajaraja's lord (Shiva).' This name is recorded in over 100 inscriptions on the temple walls. The more commonly used name 'Brihadeeswarar' (the Great Lord — an epithet of Shiva) came into prevalent use later.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: 'Peruvudaiyar Kovil' ('temple of the great possessor/lord') is a genuine colloquial Tamil name for the temple, still used locally, but it is not the original formal inscriptional name given by Rajaraja Chola I.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: 'Dakshina Meru Prasadam' is a poetic descriptive epithet meaning 'gift of the southern Meru' — it refers to the temple's grandeur but was never its formal name in inscriptions.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: 'Shivapadashekara Kshetram' is a fabricated formal name combining the king's devotional title with a generic sacred-site term — this combination does not appear in inscriptions.

Value Addition:
• The shift from 'Rajarajeshvaram' to 'Brihadeeswarar' in popular usage illustrates how temples acquire new names over centuries as their cultural context evolves.
• All of Rajaraja Chola I's inscriptions use the regnal title 'Rajakesarivarman' as the king's name in formal records.
• The discovery of the inscriptions' content in the 19th–20th centuries by epigraphists of the Archaeological Survey of India transformed scholarly understanding of Chola administrative history.

solution.concept_anchor: Chola cultural influence — Bhakti, SE Asia, merchant guilds, Nayanmars

statement_analysis.statement: The 63 Nayanmars were exclusively Brahmin saint-poets who composed the Tevaram hymns as part of the Shaiva Bhakti tradition in Tamil Nadu.
statement_analysis.reason: The 63 Nayanmars came from diverse social backgrounds — they included people from Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vellalar, artisan, and even lower-caste communities. The Bhakti movement's hallmark was its cross-caste character; 'exclusively Brahmin' is a scope-extension falsehood.

statement_analysis.statement: Chola-period temple architecture and religious practices were transmitted to Southeast Asian courts and ports partly through the agency of Tamil merchant guilds maintaining long-distance trade networks.
statement_analysis.reason: This is an established position in South and Southeast Asian historiography — Tamil merchant guilds (Ayyavole, Manigramam) operated across maritime Southeast Asia and served as non-state carriers of Chola cultural influence.

statement_analysis.statement: The Alvars were Vaishnava saint-poets whose devotional compositions are distinct from the Nayanmars' Tevaram; the Chola kings primarily patronised the Shaiva Nayanmars tradition, though some Chola rulers also supported Vaishnava temples.
statement_analysis.reason: The Alvars/Vaishnava vs. Nayanmars/Shaiva distinction and the Chola dynasty's predominantly Shaiva patronage (with some exceptions) are accurate — this reflects the documented religious policy of the dynasty.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) including all three is chosen by students who accept Statement 1 without scrutiny — the 'Brahmin only' qualifier is the scope-extension trap, and students who associate Bhakti scholarship with Brahmin learning may not flag this as the error.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The Nayanmars came from diverse castes — not exclusively Brahmin. The Bhakti movement is precisely characterised by its cross-caste inclusivity (Appar was a Vellalar, Nandanar was from a lower caste, etc.). Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: Tamil merchant guild agency in Southeast Asian cultural transmission is well-documented. Statement 2 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: Alvars = Vaishnava, Nayanmars = Shaiva; Chola patronage was primarily Shaiva — accurate. Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 2 and 3 are correct; Statement 1 is incorrect — answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 uses a scope-extension trap: adding 'exclusively Brahmin' to the Nayanmars' social composition makes a true statement false. The Bhakti movement's defining social feature was precisely its cross-caste composition — saints from all social backgrounds were included. Students who associate 'Sanskrit learning' or 'temple liturgy' with Brahmin exclusivity may unconsciously extend this to the Bhakti saints, accepting Statement 1 without questioning the 'exclusively' qualifier.
solution.final_explanation:
Chola-era religious and cultural dynamics span the Bhakti movement, maritime trade, and patronage politics — all three are tested here.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The 63 Nayanmars were emphatically NOT exclusively Brahmin. The cross-caste composition of the Nayanmars is one of the Bhakti movement's most significant social features. The 63 include people from Brahmin, Vellalar, warrior, artisan, fisherman, and other communities — including at least one woman (Karaikkal Ammaiyar). Nandanar, among the most celebrated, is said to have come from a low-caste background. The 'exclusively Brahmin' claim fundamentally misrepresents the Bhakti tradition.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Tamil merchant guilds — particularly Ayyavole (also known as the Five Hundred of Aihole/Ayyavolu) and Manigramam — maintained trading posts across the Indian Ocean rim and into Southeast Asia. Their presence facilitated the spread of South Indian religious practices, iconographic styles, and architectural traditions.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Nayanmars (Shaiva) and Alvars (Vaishnava) represent two parallel but distinct Tamil Bhakti streams. Chola kings were predominantly Shaiva (Rajaraja Chola I's title Shivapadashekara is emblematic), though individual Chola rulers occasionally patronised Vaishnava temples — reflecting pragmatic religious pluralism within a broadly Shaiva royal ideology.

Value Addition:
• Karaikkal Ammaiyar is the only woman among the 63 Nayanmars — her compositions are among the earliest devotional poetry in Tamil.
• The Tevaram hymns form books 1–7 of the Tirumurai; the remaining books include the compositions of other Shaiva saints and philosophers.
• Inscriptions of the Ayyavole guild have been found at sites in present-day Thailand, Malaysia, and Indonesia — demonstrating their geographic reach.

solution.concept_anchor: Rajaraja Chola I — sequence of conquest, temple, and inscription activities
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) places temple inscriptions before the military campaigns, which students might accept on the logic that early administrative records were made during construction — not recognising that the inscriptions documenting conquest were made after the conquests occurred.
elimination_logic: Establish the chronological anchor: Rajaraja Chola I reigned 985–1014 CE. The major Sri Lanka campaign is dated to around 993–1014 CE. The temple was consecrated around 1010 CE.
Military campaigns in Sri Lanka, Kerala, and the Maldives: these are conquest campaigns that preceded the temple's consecration — conquest funded construction.
Brihadeeswarar temple consecration: ~1010 CE — after the major campaigns, which funded it.

Tevaram recovery and compilation: Rajaraja had the hymns compiled and instituted at the temple — this is part of the temple's inaugural cultural programme, at or after consecration. Correct order: Military campaigns → Temple consecration → Tevaram institutionalisation → Administrative inscriptions recording all of the above. Answer: option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap operates on the relationship between the military campaigns and the temple construction. Students might reasonably assume that administrative/religious activities began early in the reign (before major campaigns), placing inscriptions or Tevaram recovery before the conquests. In fact, the Digvijaya ideology dictates that temple construction is the commemoration of conquest — conquest precedes construction, and inscriptions recording conquest are made at or after the temple's establishment.
solution.final_explanation:
The sequence of Rajaraja Chola I's major activities reveals the ideological and practical logic of Chola temple building.

**Correct sequence:** Military campaigns (Sri Lanka, Kerala, Maldives) → Temple construction and consecration (~1010 CE) → Tevaram compilation and institutionalisation → Administrative inscriptions recording donations and conquests

• Military campaigns (first): The Digvijaya ideology required conquest to precede commemoration. Wealth from Sri Lanka (Anuradhapura), Kerala, and the Maldives financed the construction of Brihadeeswarar. Campaigns spanned roughly 993–1010 CE.
• Temple consecration (~1010 CE): The Brihadeeswarar was consecrated around 1010 CE — the physical monument to imperial victory.
• Tevaram institutionalisation (at/after consecration): Rajaraja Chola I's 'rediscovery' of the Tevaram hymns and their formal installation as the liturgical tradition of Brihadeeswarar was part of the temple's inaugural cultural programme.
• Administrative inscriptions (ongoing, but recorded after events): The inscriptions documenting donations, land grants, and military conquests were carved over the years following consecration — they are records of accomplished facts, not prospective plans.

Value Addition:
• The Anuradhapura campaign in Sri Lanka was particularly significant — Rajaraja Chola I effectively dismantled the northern Sri Lankan kingdom and installed a Chola administration.
• Inscription-dating shows that the Brihadeeswarar inscriptions were added over several years, suggesting the temple's administrative and liturgical programme was still being formalised in the years after the 1010 CE consecration.
• The link between military victory and religious commemoration is a pattern repeated across Indian dynasties — the Vijayanagara kings later used similar Digvijaya symbolism.

solution.concept_anchor: Dravidian vs. Nagara — architectural order distinctions

statement_analysis.statement: The Nagara style of temple architecture, found predominantly in northern India, is characterised by a curvilinear tower (shikhara) above the garbhagriha, in contrast to the Dravidian style's stepped pyramidal vimana.
statement_analysis.reason: The Nagara/curvilinear vs. Dravidian/pyramidal distinction is the foundational classification of Indian temple architecture — this description is accurate.

statement_analysis.statement: The 'Vesara' style of temple architecture is a purely Chola innovation that combines the Nagara and Dravidian orders, and all examples of Vesara architecture are found exclusively within the present-day state of Tamil Nadu.
statement_analysis.reason: The Vesara style is primarily associated with the Deccan region (Karnataka, parts of Andhra Pradesh) — it is not a Chola innovation, and it is definitely not confined to Tamil Nadu. Chalukya and Hoysala temples are canonical examples of Vesara.

statement_analysis.statement: The comparison between the Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram and the Brihadeeswarar at Thanjavur illustrates a development in scale, material, and iconographic complexity from the Pallava to the Chola period in South Indian temple architecture.
statement_analysis.reason: This accurately describes the Pallava-to-Chola evolution: Shore Temple (sandstone, smaller scale, 8th century Pallava) vs. Brihadeeswarar (granite, vastly larger scale, 1010 CE Chola) — the comparison is a valid and commonly cited architectural development narrative.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) 'Statement 2 only is NOT correct' is the answer — but students who know Vesara is associated with the Deccan and is not Chola may hesitate if they confuse 'Vesara' with the Chola contribution to the mixed style, particularly if they half-remember 'Chalukyan Vesara' without locating it precisely.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 2: Vesara is the Deccan mixed style, associated with the Chalukyas and Hoysalas of Karnataka — NOT a Chola innovation, and NOT confined to Tamil Nadu. Both claims in Statement 2 are wrong. Statement 2 is NOT correct.
Evaluate Statement 1: Nagara curvilinear vs. Dravidian pyramidal — this is the canonical distinction. Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: Shore Temple (Pallava) → Brihadeeswarar (Chola) as an architectural development narrative — accurate. Statement 3 is correct.

Only Statement 2 is NOT correct — answer is (a)... checking options: the option matching 'Statement 2 only' in an 'incorrect' framing must be identified. For a 3-statement question with options (a) 1 and 2 only NOT correct, (b) 2 only NOT correct... this needs to use standard 3-statement option patterns but for an incorrect stem. Answer: the option that names Statement 2 only = (b) based on the format used.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses a scope-extension trap in two ways: first, it attributes Vesara to the Cholas (wrong — it is Chalukyan-Hoysala); second, it claims Vesara is confined to Tamil Nadu (wrong — it is the Deccan). The Cholas contributed to Dravidian architecture's mature phase — they did not create the Vesara style. Students with broad but imprecise coverage of Indian temple architecture orders may accept 'Chola = mixed style' reasoning without fixing the geographic and dynastic specificity of Vesara.
solution.final_explanation:
The three principal orders of Indian temple architecture — Nagara, Dravidian, Vesara — must be precisely located by dynasty and region.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Nagara (northern) style uses a curvilinear shikhara; Dravidian (southern) style uses a multi-storeyed stepped pyramidal vimana. This is the foundational classification and is accurately stated.
• Statement 2 — NOT Correct: The Vesara style is not a Chola innovation. 'Vesara' (meaning 'mixed' or 'mule') describes the blend of Nagara and Dravidian elements found primarily in the Deccan — especially in Chalukya (Badami, Pattadakal) and Hoysala (Belur, Halebidu) temples in present-day Karnataka. It has nothing to do with Chola Tamil Nadu. The 'exclusively Tamil Nadu' geographic claim is also completely false.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Shore Temple (Pallava, sandstone, early 8th century, modest scale) compared to the Brihadeeswarar (Chola, granite, 66m vimana, 1010 CE) is the standard illustration of the evolution from early experimental Dravidian architecture to its mature Chola form.

Value Addition:
• Pattadakal (Karnataka, a UNESCO WHS) is the best site for comparing Nagara, Dravidian, and Vesara styles at a single location.
• Hoysala architecture is the finest example of late Vesara — with star-shaped (stellate) plans and lathe-turned decorative detail.
• The Chola vimana's multi-storeyed tala system became the model for South Indian temple architecture in the Vijayanagara and later periods.

solution.concept_anchor: Rajendra Chola I Srivijaya campaign — Kadaram geographic identification
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because Anuradhapura is the correct target of a Chola military campaign — but it was Rajaraja Chola I's Sri Lanka campaign, not Rajendra Chola I's Srivijaya campaign. Attributing Anuradhapura to Rajendra I's naval campaign involves a geographic-swap that swaps the king along with the target.
elimination_logic: Identify what Rajendra Chola I's naval campaign (~1025 CE) targeted: the Srivijaya empire — whose capital Kadaram is identified with sites in present-day Malaysia or southern Thailand (Kedah/Takuapa).
Eliminate option (a): Anuradhapura (Sri Lanka) was the target of Rajaraja Chola I's campaign, not Rajendra I's Srivijaya naval expedition.
Eliminate option (b): The Malabar coast (Kerala) was a target of Rajaraja Chola I — not associated with Rajendra's Srivijaya campaign.

Eliminate option (d): The Ganges plains — while Rajendra I did campaign northward to the Ganga (earning his title Gangaikonda), that was a different campaign from the 1025 CE naval Srivijaya expedition. Kadaram/Srivijaya is the correct target — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap operates between different Chola military targets. Both Rajaraja I and Rajendra I conducted major military campaigns, but their targets were different: Rajaraja's naval campaigns targeted Sri Lanka (Anuradhapura) and the Maldives; Rajendra's famous naval expedition (~1025 CE) targeted Kadaram (the Srivijaya capital, located in present-day Malaysia/southern Thailand). Students who associate 'Chola naval power' with 'Sri Lanka' may incorrectly apply the Anuradhapura target to Rajendra's campaign — a geographic-swap that confuses the two kings' campaigns.
solution.final_explanation:
The distinction between Rajaraja Chola I's and Rajendra Chola I's military targets is a high-probability UPSC exam distinction.

• Option (a) — Incorrectly matched: Anuradhapura was the target of Rajaraja Chola I's Sri Lanka campaign, not Rajendra Chola I's Srivijaya naval expedition. Attributing Anuradhapura to Rajendra I is a geographic-swap error.
• Option (b) — Incorrectly matched: The Malabar coast (Kerala/Chera kingdom) was targeted by Rajaraja Chola I as part of his consolidation of the South Indian peninsula — not a target of Rajendra I's Southeast Asian naval campaign.
• Option (c) — Correctly matched: Rajendra Chola I's c.1025 CE naval expedition targeted the Srivijaya empire, whose capital Kadaram is identified with sites in present-day Malaysia or southern Thailand (Kedah or Takuapa). This is one of the most spectacular pre-modern Indian naval operations — ships crossed the Bay of Bengal to attack a maritime empire thousands of kilometres away.
• Option (d) — Incorrectly matched: The Gangetic plains were the target of Rajendra I's famous northward land campaign (not the 1025 CE naval expedition). That campaign earned him the title 'Gangaikonda' but is a different military operation from the Srivijaya naval expedition.

Value Addition:
• The Srivijaya empire was the dominant maritime power in Southeast Asia controlling the Straits of Malacca — Rajendra's campaign was likely motivated by trade rivalry.
• 'Kadaram' appears in Rajendra Chola I's inscriptions as the name of the Srivijaya capital targeted — its exact identification with modern geography (Kedah in Malaysia or Takuapa in Thailand) remains debated.
• The distance covered by Rajendra's fleet — crossing from the Coromandel coast to Southeast Asia — makes it one of the longest naval campaigns in pre-modern world history.

solution.concept_anchor: Chola artistic sources — primary source types and their content

statement_analysis.statement: Brihadeeswarar inscriptions — Primary source for Rajaraja Chola I's military campaigns, land grants (devadana), and the socio-economic organisation of the temple as an employer of hundreds of staff
statement_analysis.reason: The Brihadeeswarar inscriptions in Tamil and Grantha scripts are exactly this — the primary source for military, administrative, and social historical data from Rajaraja Chola I's reign.

statement_analysis.statement: Chola bronze sculptures (utsava murtis) — Primary source for understanding the iconographic codification of Shaiva deities and the technical sophistication of the panchaloha lost-wax casting tradition
statement_analysis.reason: The surviving Chola bronzes are the primary material evidence for the iconographic programme and metallurgical tradition — they are direct, unmediated primary sources for these aspects of Chola civilisation.

statement_analysis.statement: Brihadeeswarar Chola-period murals — Primary source for Chola literary production, including the complete texts of the Tevaram hymns as originally recited at the temple
statement_analysis.reason: The Chola murals depict visual subjects (Shaiva Puranic scenes, royal portraiture of Rajaraja and Karuvurar) — they are not a textual source and do not contain the Tevaram hymns. The Tevaram's transmission was through manuscripts and oral tradition, not murals.

statement_analysis.statement: Silpa shastra texts (e.g., Manasara, Mayamata) — Secondary/prescriptive sources that guided Chola craftsmen by specifying iconographic rules for sculpture and proportional canons for temple construction
statement_analysis.reason: The silpa shastras are prescriptive texts — they guided craftsmen but are secondary/normative sources, not primary records of specific Chola events. Their classification as prescriptive/secondary relative to inscriptions and material artefacts is accurate.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' is chosen by students who incorrectly accept Statement 3, reasoning that murals 'must contain religious texts' because murals depict religious themes. The conflation of visual religious content with textual religious source is the trap.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 3: The Brihadeeswarar murals depict Shaiva Puranic scenes and royal portraits — they are visual art, not textual records. The complete Tevaram texts were transmitted through manuscripts and oral recitation, not painted on walls. Statement 3 is incorrect.

Evaluate Statements 1, 2, 4: Inscriptions as primary sources for conquest and economy — correct. Bronzes as primary sources for iconography and metallurgy — correct. Silpa shastras as prescriptive secondary sources — correct.
Three pairs are correct, one is incorrect — answer is 'Only three' — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 uses a conflation trap: students conflate 'religious murals' with 'religious text sources.' The Chola murals are visual records of mythology and royal history — they are valuable primary sources for art history and visual culture, but they do not contain the Tevaram's textual content. The Tevaram hymns are literary/musical compositions transmitted through manuscripts and the oral tradition of trained singers (oduvar), not inscribed or painted on temple walls. Equating visual religious iconography with textual religious content is the conflation.
solution.final_explanation:
Classifying different types of historical sources and understanding what each can and cannot tell us is a key skill for UPSC's history questions.

| Pair | Source | What it provides | Verdict |
|------|--------|------------------|---------|
| 1 | Brihadeeswarar inscriptions | Military history, land grants, temple economy | Correct |
| 2 | Chola bronzes (utsava murtis) | Iconographic codification, lost-wax technique | Correct |
| 3 | Chola murals — Tevaram hymn texts | Visual Puranic and royal scenes, NOT hymn texts | Incorrect |
| 4 | Silpa shastra texts | Prescriptive guide for craftsmen | Correct |

Statement 3 is wrong: the Chola murals depict visual subjects — Shaiva mythological scenes and royal portraiture including Rajaraja Chola I with his guru Karuvurar. They are valuable as primary visual sources for iconographic and social history, but they do not contain or transmit the literary/musical content of the Tevaram. Three pairs are correctly described — answer is 'Only three.'

Value Addition:
• The oduvar tradition — trained singers who recite Tevaram in temples — is the living continuation of the liturgical practice instituted by Rajaraja Chola I at Brihadeeswarar.
• Primary sources for Chola history include: inscriptions (stone and copper plate), bronze sculptures, architecture itself (spatial organisation), and foreign accounts (Arab and Chinese travellers).
• Manasara and Mayamata are the two most cited silpa shastra texts for South Indian temple architecture — they cover everything from site selection to proportional canons to iconographic details.
